notes.body:
Two very different kinds of wrong leadership appear in the passage, and the line between them is doctrinal, not merely moral. الناصب is someone who has actively planted **enmity against the People of the House (أهل البيت)** — the Prophet's family and the chain of Imams. الحروري takes its name from Harura (حَرُورَاء), near Kufa, where الخوارج first broke from Maulana Ali, declaring him a disbeliever and seeking his death. Both have cut themselves off, at the root, from the Imam's spiritual authority.

This is why the instruction is almost architectural: **treat him as one of the pillars of the mosque** — not a leader, not a conduit, just stone. You recite for yourself as if alone, because spiritually you are alone. A person who has turned against the Imams carries no light to pass to those praying behind them.

The "unjust" imam discussed immediately afterward is something else entirely. He is a summoner — a داعي — within the true hierarchy whose conduct has failed but who has never renounced the Imam or declared war on the People of the House (أهل البيت). His fault is **conduct, not creed** — and prayer behind him is obligatory.

Dissimulation (تقية) is the principle that holds this together, and what lifts it above a legal convenience is that **the Imams named it as their religion**:

التقية ديني ودين آبائي
Dissimulation is my religion and the religion of my fathers.

Even Imam al-Husayn ibn Ali allowed Muawiya's governor to lead prayer over al-Hasan, saying only that the practice compelled it. The community is not passive, though — when injustice appears in a summoner, they must bring it before the holder of authority and await judgment.

The contrast is this:

- الناصب and الحروري have broken with الإمامة at the creedal level — prayer behind them is spiritually null.
- The unjust summoner has bent in conduct but remains within the living hierarchy — prayer is valid; the wrong must be reported.

A spiritual leader is meant to be a window through whom the Imam's light reaches those who pray. When someone has **closed that window from the inside** by making the Imams their enemies, they become exactly what the instruction calls them: a pillar — part of the building, and nothing more.
notes.anchor: Do not count the prayer behind a الناصب or a الحروري as valid
notes.quote: Do not count the prayer behind a الناصب or a الحروري as valid
etymology: ناصب (enemy of أهل البيت): from the root ن-ص-ب, meaning to erect, set up, or plant firmly. The active participle نَاصِب describes one who has "erected" a thing — here, hostility toward the Imams as a fixed, deliberate stance. Think of a stake driven into the ground: this figure has planted enmity and left it standing.

الحروري (Kharijite): named after Harura (حَرُورَاء), a town near Kufa where الخوارج first broke from Maulana Ali after the Battle of Siffin. The place name connects to حَرّ, meaning intense heat — fitting for a movement ablaze with its own certainty. They declared Maulana Ali a disbeliever and sought his death.

تقية (dissimulation): from the root و-ق-ي, meaning to guard or shield. The same root gives وِقَايَة (protection) and the verb اتَّقَى (to guard oneself, to exercise deep reverence for Allah). The term describes guarding one's inner faith under pressure — letting the outer conform while the heart remains aligned with the Imam.

جائر (unjust): from the root ج-و-ر, meaning to deviate or veer off course. The noun جَوْر is injustice understood as a swerving from uprightness. A جائر is one whose conduct has bent off-line — though in this passage he remains within the community's living hierarchy and has not broken with the Imams.

notes.body:
The answer rests on a principle Islamic jurisprudence has always held: **representation ends the instant the represented party arrives**. A deputy (نائب) holds his office because his principal is absent; the moment the principal appears, the gap simply closes.

Think of a manager left to run a company while the owner is abroad — **the authority is lent, and lending ends on return**. The moment the owner walks through the door, the manager cannot chair a session 'on behalf of' someone sitting right there in the room.

The preacher was in exactly this position. At some earlier point, the man who entered had granted him permission (إذن) to occupy that pulpit. The summons (دعوة) operates this way at every level:

1. The Imam authorizes his proof (حجة).
2. The proof authorizes the summoner (داعي).
3. The summoner licenses the authorized one (مأذون) below him.

Once the authorizing rank is physically present, the lower rank cannot act 'on its behalf.' Each holder of office preaches only because the rank above breathed authority into him; **no rank in the chain is self-appointing**.

The man who entered had once placed the preacher in that pulpit, in effect saying: 'lead in my name.' That single act made him the preacher's master — not on the day he walked through the door, but from **the very first sermon**.
notes.anchor: that preacher is the property of the man who entered through the door…
notes.quote: that preacher is the property of the man who entered through the door of the congregational mosque, for that man had appointed him as his deputy
etymology: نائب (deputy): from root ن-و-ب, meaning to rotate, alternate, or take turns. A نائب is one who 'comes in another's turn' — standing where the principal would stand, in the principal's absence. The root quietly marks deputyship as inherently temporary: when the original holder returns, the نائب's turn is simply over.

إذن (permission): from root أ-ذ-ن, whose core sense is the ear (أُذُن). To grant إذن is to 'lend your ear' — to hear and approve. Permission, in this root, is not merely a formal clearance; it is an act of attentive reception, a bending of the higher rank toward the one below before authorizing them to act.

دعوة (the summons): from root د-ع-و, meaning to call or invite. The root yields دَعَا (he called), دُعَاء (supplication — calling upon Allah), and دَاعِي (the one who calls). In the Ismaili context, the summons is a living chain of calling: each rank calls the one below toward the Imam, as the Imam calls toward Allah.

حجة (proof): from root ح-ج-ج, which also gives حَجَّ (to make pilgrimage — to move toward a sacred destination). The حجة demonstrates the Imam's truth by their very presence, as a destination proves a journey was real. The root links argument with arrival: proof is not merely logical; it is a presence you travel toward.

notes.body:
The twenty-three magnifications (تكبير) rest on a straightforward sum: ten spiritual ranks, ten bodily ranks, and three specific persons — the speaker of the cycle (ناطق), his executor or foundation (أساس), and the Imam of the age. That is 10 + 10 + 3 = **twenty-three**.

The ten spiritual ranks refer to the hierarchy of the unseen, luminous world — the chain of spiritual intelligences that Ismaili cosmology describes as the structure of reality above the material plane. The ten bodily ranks are their living mirror: the chain of summoners who carry the call (دعوة) outward from the Imam through every level of society to reach the seeker. Together these twenty ranks **map the full architecture of creation**, from its highest, most luminous origin down to the most earthly expression.

The three named figures — the speaker (ناطق), the executor (أساس), and the Imam of the age — are not abstract stations but living persons: the one who delivers the outward law, the one who carries its inner meaning, and **the Imam** as the present axis around whom both orbit. In every prophetic cycle, these three have been the irreducible poles of divine authority.

The five great prophets — the possessors of firm resolve (أولو العزم) — and the five daily prayers they correspond to do not add to the count. They **supply the frame**: each daily prayer is a re-enactment of one prophetic cycle, and all five together rehearse the complete arc of divine summons across history. The magnifications of the festival days are therefore reckoned against this full picture — not one cycle alone, but the sweep of all five speakers and the twenty-three ranks and persons their summons contains.

When we raise our hands in magnification during those blessed days, each repetition is not empty ceremony — it is an acknowledgment, count by count, of the entire living structure through which **the mercy of Allah reaches us**.
notes.anchor: it is a likeness of what obtains in the summons of the five speakers…
notes.quote: it is a likeness of what obtains in the summons of the five speakers — the possessors of firm resolve — who correspond to the five prayers, drawn from the mention of the ten spiritual ranks and the ten bodily ranks, and the mention of the speaker of the cycle, his executor, and the Imam of the age
etymology: تكبير: from the root ك-ب-ر, meaning to be great or vast in measure and standing. The form تكبير names the act of declaring that greatness — the utterance اللهُ أَكْبَر. The root's core sense of immeasurable magnitude flows directly into the gesture: every magnification is a proclamation that Allah's greatness exceeds all comparison.

عزم: the heart of أولو العزم; from ع-ز-م, meaning to resolve with unflinching firmness and to commit without retreat. عزم is the quality of a decision that does not waver once made. أولو العزم — those who hold this quality — are the five great prophets distinguished not only by their mission but by the steel of their inner resolve.

ناطق: from ن-ط-ق, meaning to produce distinct, articulate sound — not mere noise but intelligible, clear speech. The Ismaili ناطق is the prophet who articulates divine will into a law human beings can hear and follow. The root captures both the physical act of clear enunciation and the higher act of making the hidden knowable through spoken form.

حدود: from ح-د-د, meaning to mark a sharp boundary or limit. A حدّ is a defined edge between two things. In the summons hierarchy, the حدود are precise stations within the chain of authority — defined boundaries so that each summoner occupies exactly the place appointed, neither overreaching above nor falling short below.
